title: Research Explained #29 -- Can We Change Spacetime Without Moving Matter?
html:
Imagine two sealed boxes bolted to a bench. One stores light in a cavity. We transfer some of that energy to the other box and wait for the equipment to settle. The boxes stay in place. Would nearby clocks register a change?

General relativity predicts that the clocks’ rates relative to each other would change in this idealized setup. Energy has moved from one location to another, even though we never slid a heavy object across the bench. The catch is the size of the effect. In an idealized example below, moving a million joules between two fixed reservoirs changes the clocks' relative rates by about one part in 1037.

Research Explained #28 asked how we might detect an artificial change in spacetime. Here we ask what could cause one, how much change ordinary physics predicts, and what a measurement would have to rule out.

What Einstein's equation counts

In modern notation, Einstein's field equation is

Gμν + Λ gμν = (8π G/c4)Tμν.

Here gμν describes spacetime geometry, Gμν is the Einstein tensor, Λ is the cosmological constant, G is Newton's gravitational constant, and c is the vacuum speed of light. The stress-energy tensor Tμν keeps track of energy density, energy flow and momentum density, and stresses such as pressure, tension and shear. In a local orthonormal frame its components have units of energy per volume. The factor G/c4 has units of length per energy, so the source side has units of inverse length squared, as curvature does. The field equation fixes the Ricci part of curvature locally through the source. Tidal curvature can also extend through empty space, as it does outside Earth. A region outside Earth can be nearly empty and still have tides. Freely falling objects there can accelerate relative to each other. Einstein, The Foundation of the General Theory of Relativity (1916), Einstein, Cosmological Considerations in the General Theory of Relativity (1917)

A magnetic field has energy density uB=B2/(2μ0), where B is magnetic flux density in tesla and μ0 is the vacuum permeability. A pure magnetic field also exerts pressure across the field and tension along it. Those stresses matter. In the stationary linearized limit the potential governing slow test bodies and stationary clocks obeys ∇2Φ=4π G(T00+∑i Tii)/c2, using x0=ct, with t the time coordinate, and locally Cartesian background coordinates after removing the fixed background contribution. Here Φ is the gravitational potential in the stationary weak-field approximation, T₀₀ is energy density and the three Tᵢᵢ terms are stresses along the coordinate axes. In a field-only region the magnetic contribution to the combination in parentheses is 2uB.

To predict gravity outside a real magnet, the source must include the conductors, supports, return field, and energy supply. Electromagnetic forces exchange momentum with matter, so the field's stress-energy alone generally fails the conservation condition at those interfaces. For a stationary, isolated, weakly gravitating assembly, the volume integral of each stress component vanishes at leading order when the boundary traction term vanishes, and the distant monopole tracks total energy divided by c2. Tolman, On the Weight of Heat and Thermal Equilibrium in General Relativity (1930), Misner and Putnam, Active Gravitational Mass (1959), Giulini (2018), Laue’s theorem

For scale, an idealized 10-tesla field filling one litre stores about 40 kilojoules in that volume. This assumes a uniform field there and counts only that volume. André Füzfa calculated the geometry around idealized current loops and solenoids and proposed a measurement. The numerical model neglects the mass of the wires and charge carriers. A prediction for a specific apparatus needs its full source and detector model. Füzfa, How Current Loops and Solenoids Curve Spacetime (2016)

What a million joules would do

Start with a compact, stationary assembly that has received a net increment U of stored energy. For this first calculation, treat the supplying reservoir as remote and calculate the assembly's incremental gravity alone. Far outside the assembly but near enough that the supply contribution can be neglected or accounted for separately, the leading terms are

Δ M = U/c2,
δΦ(r) = −GU/(c2r),
|δ a(r)| = GU/(c2r2).

At r=0.10 m, with U=1.0 MJ and source size much smaller than r, the added mass equivalent is 1.1×10−11 kg, about 11 nanograms. The extra inward acceleration is 7.4×10−20 m s−2. Two nearby freely falling probes would acquire a radial relative acceleration per unit separation of 2GU/(c2r3), about 1.5×10−18 s−2. That last quantity is a tidal observable. A supported accelerometer instead measures proper acceleration, which can change when its mount moves. Einstein (1916), NIST CODATA constants

Now put the supply back in the picture. Place identical compact reservoirs A and B one metre apart, and put a clock 10 centimetres inboard of each. Each clock is then 90 centimetres from the other reservoir. Compare stationary configurations before and after transferring U from B to A. Assume weak gravity and fixed positions in both settled states. Treat each reservoir’s settled energy change, including its local confinement, as a compact mass increment at its center. This calculation includes those two contributions and assumes that changes in the rest of the apparatus make negligible contributions to the clock difference. For matched stationary clocks in the weak field, the fractional rate difference y=(νA−νB)/ν, with ν the common nominal frequency, changes from the initial to the final settled state by

δ y = (δΦA − δΦB)/c2
= −(2GU/c4)(1/(0.10 m) − 1/(0.90 m))
≈ −1.5 × 10−37.

Clock A runs more slowly relative to clock B after the transfer. Reversing the transfer reverses the change. The two idealized mass increments sum to zero at this order. An isolated apparatus must also conserve its total momentum and center of energy, so the far-field pattern must include any compensating motion or energy redistribution. The center of energy moves uniformly for an isolated system at this order, so it stays fixed in that system’s rest frame. In a mounted experiment the bench and its surroundings can take up momentum and strain. Modeling the transfer itself requires the time-dependent energy flow and a gravitational response that propagates causally. Einstein (1916), Giulini (2018)

Bothwell and colleagues measured a frequency gradient consistent with Earth’s gravitational redshift across a millimetre-scale sample of ultracold strontium. Their comparison between two regions of that sample reached a statistical fractional frequency uncertainty of 7.6 × 10⁻²¹ after 92 hours. That is about 5 × 10¹⁶ times the calculated two-reservoir signal in magnitude. A vertical millimetre on Earth gives a fractional shift of about 1.1 × 10⁻¹⁹. The comparison uses the reported uncertainty from their specific clock protocol. Bothwell et al. (2022), Fig. 4 and Extended Data Table 1, accepted manuscript

Westphal and colleagues used a torsion balance to resolve gravity between millimetre-sized gold spheres by periodically moving a source of about 90 milligrams. These measurements give a sense of scale for the specific setups in which they were made. Westphal et al. (2021)

What about vacuum energy?

“Vacuum energy” can refer to two very different comparisons. A Lorentz-invariant contribution with energy density uvac has Tμνvac=−uvacgμν in the (−+++) convention, with pressure p=−uvac. A uniform term of that form enters the field equation like a cosmological constant. Under the standard flat cosmological model with a cosmological constant and cold dark matter, Planck measurements combined with baryon acoustic oscillation data imply an effective energy density of about 5.3 × 10⁻¹⁰ joules per cubic metre. The inference concerns cosmic expansion and depends on the cosmological model. How the observed effective constant arises from microscopic physics is the cosmological constant problem. Planck Collaboration VI (2020), Table 2, Weinberg, The Cosmological Constant Problem (1989)

The Casimir effect concerns an energy difference associated with boundaries. For ideal, perfectly conducting parallel plates of area A, separated by a gap d, at zero temperature and neglecting edges, the interaction energy per area is −π2ℏ c/(720d3), with ℏ the reduced Planck constant. Dividing by d gives a gap-averaged interaction energy density of about −4.3×10−4 J m−3 at d=1 μm, relative to the chosen no-interaction reference. The magnitude is 10,000 times smaller when the gap grows tenfold, so the negative density approaches zero. Its units follow from ℏ c having units of joule-metres. Real plates bring finite conductivity, temperature, geometry and electrostatic corrections. Casimir, original parallel-plate calculation (1948)

Lamoreaux used a torsion pendulum to measure the Casimir force between a curved lens and a plate. In a separate calculation, Fulling and colleagues found that the negative interaction energy of ideal parallel plates reduces the cavity’s predicted weight in an external gravitational field. A weight measurement would probe the cavity’s response to that field. A measurement of the gravity it generates would probe a different observable. Either experiment would need to account for the rest of the apparatus. The Casimir force can also be formulated using interactions of the material charges, so a force measurement alone does not identify an absolute vacuum energy density. Lamoreaux (1997), Lamoreaux erratum (1998), Fulling et al. (2007), Jaffe (2005)

How much negative energy can persist?

In some quantum states the renormalized energy density measured by an observer can fall below its vacuum reference. Quantum energy inequalities put lower bounds on certain time averages. For a free, massless, minimally coupled scalar field in four-dimensional flat spacetime without boundaries, Ford and Roman's Lorentzian-sampled bound for an inertial observer is

∫−∞∞ [τ0 dτ/(π(τ2 + τ02))] ⟨u(τ)⟩ren
≥ −3ℏ/(32π2c3τ04).

The sampling weight integrates to one, and τ and τ0 are proper time and sampling width in seconds. The weight is largest near the midpoint and tapers away on both sides. The bound applies to the whole weighted average. The lower bound is about −3.7×10−26 J m−3 at one nanosecond. At one microsecond it is a trillion times closer to zero. These are lower bounds on weighted averages in the stated theory. Field type, boundary conditions, curvature and sampling matter. In particular, applying this boundary-free scalar formula directly to the electromagnetic Casimir gap would give a spurious comparison. Fewster and Eveson derived bounds for other sampling functions in flat-spacetime scalar theory. Applying such results to wormholes adds assumptions about the geometry, quantum source and semiclassical gravity. Ford and Roman (1996), §2, Eq. (1), Fewster and Eveson (1998)

Classical Maxwell fields obey the null energy condition, which tests a contraction of the full stress-energy tensor along lightlike directions. More magnetic energy alone therefore cannot supply a source that requires violation of that condition. In a theoretical model, Gao, Jafferis and Wall explicitly coupled the two boundaries of an eternal black hole in anti-de Sitter spacetime. The resulting quantum stress opens a path through the model’s bridge while preserving causality in that setup. A laboratory source would need its own physically realizable stress-energy, formation mechanism and stability analysis. Morris and Thorne (1988), Gao, Jafferis and Wall (2017)

What would count as a test?

A first experiment would ask whether a calibrated energy redistribution produces the ordinary gravitational response predicted for the entire apparatus under general relativity (GR). The two-reservoir example supplies a sign and a scale. A real design needs the spatial pattern and time dependence as well. Differential free-fall probes could target a gravity gradient, or clock comparisons could target relative rates. Each needs a calibrated response model and a demonstration that ordinary couplings can be bounded below the effect being tested.

  • Change where the energy goes. Reverse the transfer, vary the stored energy and change detector position. Compare the measured sign, amplitude and spatial pattern with a prediction fixed before viewing the data. Include a layout where both clocks have the same predicted potential change, such as two clocks on the plane halfway between the ideal reservoirs. Symmetric inboard clocks generally have opposite potential changes. Reversal alone is weak evidence because heat, magnetic forces and motion can also reverse.
  • Run a matched dummy cycle. Reproduce drive currents, timing, dissipation and vibration as closely as possible with a different source-energy distribution. Monitor field leakage, temperatures, actual displacements and pickup on a common timebase. Use a known gravitational source to check the gravity response and inject a known signal separately to check acquisition and analysis.
  • Give a null result a numerical meaning. Choose an enhancement and a detector pattern before analyzing the data. For example, a test could ask whether the response is at least twice the general-relativity prediction, with the same direction and spatial pattern. Fit the multiplier of that signed prediction and account for uncertainty in the apparatus, detector and backgrounds. The data rule out a doubling at the stated confidence only if the upper confidence limit on that multiplier is below two. A limit that still allows the ordinary prediction leaves it unresolved. A larger signal would need to survive the dummy cycles, predict measurements in a second geometry and withstand independent replication before earning a gravitational interpretation.

In Research State v1.11, the project retained stored electromagnetic energy as a source concept and gave priority to the relativistic particle-beam branch for precursor studies. That record keeps beam-gravity detection on hold pending detector and background work. The proposed experiment would test a source response within ordinary gravity. A usable communications or propulsion mechanism would require further evidence of its own. (Beyond the Light Barrier, Beyond the Light Barrier Research State, v1.11, §§22.2–25, internal project record.)

General relativity gives a qualified yes. Transferring energy between fixed locations changes the predicted geometry. The practical question is whether a particular source can make a large enough, distinctive enough change to measure. The million-joule comparison shows why specifying the source and doing the arithmetic come before building a detector.

    detector and backgrounds. The data rule out a doubling at the stated
    confidence only if the upper confidence limit on that multiplier is below
    two. A limit that still allows the ordinary prediction leaves it unresolved.
    A larger signal would need to survive the dummy cycles, predict measurements
    in a second geometry and withstand independent replication before earning a
    gravitational interpretation.
  

  In Research State v1.11, the project retained stored electromagnetic energy as
  a source concept and gave priority to the relativistic particle-beam branch
  for precursor studies. That record keeps beam-gravity detection on hold
  pending detector and background work. The proposed experiment would test a
  source response within ordinary gravity. A usable communications or propulsion
  mechanism would require further evidence of its own. (Beyond the Light
  Barrier, Beyond the Light Barrier Research State, v1.11, §§22.2–25,
  internal project record.)

  General relativity gives a qualified yes. Transferring energy
  between fixed locations changes the predicted geometry. The practical question
  is whether a particular source can make a large enough, distinctive enough
  change to measure. The million-joule comparison shows why specifying the
  source and doing the arithmetic come before building a detector.
